activities.caption: file the invaders by type
activities.name: imPathogenBuckets

config.prompt: Five pathogen types, one tray of examples. File each:
config.why: Different entry strategies face different barriers: stomach acid and lysozyme work on all of them, but only bacteria offer the cell-wall and ribosome targets that antibiotics attack.

activities.anchor: the innate system reacts within minutes to hours
activities.caption: rebuild the innate response, step by step
activities.name: imInnateOrder

config.prompt: A splinter gets through the wall. Rebuild the innate response in order:
items: Phagocytes recognise bacterial signatures and engulf the invaders
Damaged cells and macrophages release histamine and cytokines
Blood vessels widen and leak — redness, heat, swelling, pain
Fever raises body temperature, slowing pathogen replication
Complement proteins punch holes in bacterial membranes
config.why: Fast and generic: minutes to hours, and it never improves with experience — the speed is what buys the adaptive system time.

activities.caption: true or false — the thermostat on trial
activities.name: imFeverJudge

statements.s: Fever means the immune system is malfunctioning, so it should be suppressed straight away.
statements.why: Fever is a regulated defence — the thermostat has not gone wrong.

statements.s: Raised temperature slows pathogen replication and speeds immune reactions.
statements.why: That double effect is exactly why fever is useful rather than merely uncomfortable.

statements.s: Fever becomes dangerous to the host above roughly 40 °C — the line for intervention.
statements.why: That is where the regulated defence turns against its own host.

statements.s: Innate recognition improves with experience, like the adaptive system's.
statements.why: It is generic — it cannot tell one flu strain from another and never improves.

activities.caption: one line of this clonal-selection summary is wrong
activities.name: imClonalSpot

config.prompt: One step of this clonal-selection walkthrough is wrong. Find it.
lines: Your body shuffles gene segments and manufactures billions of distinct B cells
Collectively they cover shapes that have never existed on Earth
The right receptor finally meets its antigen — that cell is selected
The selected cell divides into a clone of millions within minutes
This cloning plus maturation is why the primary response takes one to two weeks
config.correction: The selected cell divides into a clone of millions — but that expansion takes one to two weeks.
config.why: Clonal expansion plus cell maturation is precisely the lag you spend feeling ill; the hours-fast response only exists once memory cells are banked.

activities.anchor: The clone splits into two job descriptions
activities.caption: pair each player with its job
activities.name: imArmsMatch

config.prompt: Pair each player of the adaptive response with its job:

pairs.right: bind one antigen shape; neutralise, clump and coat invaders
coordinate — cytokines directing both B cells and killers
destroy your own cells displaying viral proteins
digest invaders, display fragments, seek the matching T cell in lymph nodes

config.why: Antibodies handle pathogens loose in blood and tissue fluids; T cells handle the ones hiding inside your own cells — and both depend on the helper T signal node, which is why lymph nodes swell.

activities.caption: drop the marker on the memory clock
activities.name: imMemoryPlace

config.prompt: Yellow-fever vaccination induces antibodies detectable how many years later? Place the marker:
config.why: Most of the clone dies when the infection clears, but memory cells persist — measles immunity from infection is effectively lifelong.

activities.anchor: first vaccine in medicine was Edward Jenner
activities.caption: run the platform decision
activities.name: imVaxBranch

config.root: You are designing a vaccine. The immune response must be the real thing — clonal expansion, antibodies, memory — but the disease cannot be. Choose each platform.

start.text: Pathogen one: a bacterium whose only weapon is a single toxin (tetanus is the classic). Which platform?

choices.label: Toxoid — the inactivated toxin alone
choices.feedback: Exactly right for this enemy — immunity to the toxin, with no way to cause disease.

choices.label: Live attenuated whole pathogen
choices.feedback: It would work, but you would be delivering the whole bacterium when only the toxin matters.

choices.label: mRNA instructions for one protein
choices.feedback: There is no viral protein here to encode — mRNA platforms speak in proteins.

toxoid.text: Pathogen two: a virus that replicates poorly when weakened (the measles/MMR strategy). Your call?

choices.label: Live attenuated strain
choices.feedback: The full antigen set, replicating too poorly to cause disease — the real response without the real illness.

choices.label: Killed whole virus, injected
choices.feedback: Also legitimate — the polio injection is a killed whole virus; a different trade-off in response strength.

live.text: Prepared defence achieved: when the genuine pathogen arrives, it is cleared before it can establish.

killed.text: Prepared defence achieved: clonal expansion has run its rehearsal either way.

live-note.text: Back up and choose the platform that presents only the inactivated toxin.

rna-note.text: Reconsider — mRNA lets your own cells manufacture one viral protein; there is none to encode for a pure toxin.

config.why: From Jenner's cowpox (1796) to mRNA, every platform is the same bargain: run clonal selection and bank memory without paying for the disease — the bargain that eradicated smallpox.

config.text: Passive immunity is %%0%% rather than made: antibodies cross the %%1%% to the foetus and arrive in %%2%%, the first milk. Antivenom works the same way — injecting ready-made antibodies. It acts %%3%% but fades in weeks, because the recipient's immune system never made the memory.
config.hint: Borrowed protection is instant but temporary — no memory cells were made.
